title: The Mystery of the Lost Amber Room
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history of the Amber Room, a Baroque room paneled with Baltic amber. It was commissioned by Frederick I of Prussia in Berlin, designed by Andreas Schlüter and built by Gottfried Wolffram, then given to Russia's Peter the First in exchange for forty grenadiers. Empress Elizabeth had it reinstalled at the Catherine Palace, Catherine the Great completed it in 1770s-1780, and the Nazis looted it in 1941 and took it to Königsberg. The room vanished after the RAF bombing and Soviet capture of Königsberg. The hosts cover theories about its fate (Wilhelm Gustloff, Jonas Valley, Weimar, Vulpera mine), the 1979 Soviet replica completed in 2003, and a listener mail segment about toast water and toast sandwiches.

segments.title: Opening and introduction to the Amber Room
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode, a listener request, and the Amber Room as a lost World War II mystery. They credit the Guardian reporters Adrian Levy and Catherine Scott-Clark's book.

segments.title: What amber is and how it forms
segments.summary: The hosts explain amber as fossilized pine resin, describe the Baltic Sea as the main source, and note how amber washes ashore after storms. They say amber was very valuable, at one point worth more than gold.

segments.title: Frederick I commissions the Amber Room
segments.summary: Frederick I of Prussia, crowned in 1701, commissions a room lined with Baltic amber for Charlottenburg Palace in Berlin. Andreas Schlüter designs it and Gottfried Wolffram carves and builds it using oak panels, bronze foil and mosaic amber, with a special adhesive.

segments.title: Firings and the gift to Peter the Great
segments.summary: Schlüter and Wolffram are both dismissed during the project. Frederick I dies, and his successor Frederick William I has the panels packed off. Peter the Great of Russia receives them in exchange for forty grenadiers, but they do not fit the palace room and are put into storage.

segments.title: Empress Elizabeth and the room's reconstruction in Russia
segments.summary: Empress Elizabeth has the room reassembled, hiring Italian sculptor Alexander Martelli, who finishes it in 1770 and keeps reworking it. The room is moved to the Catherine Palace, where it is enlarged with more amber.

segments.title: Catherine the Great completes the room
segments.summary: Catherine the Great finishes the room in 1780 with four stone mosaics depicting the senses, made by Florentine artist Giuseppe Zocchi. The hosts describe the candlelit effect and the room's craftsmanship and value.

segments.title: Nazi looting and move to Königsberg
segments.summary: After the Russian Revolution the room becomes a museum. During Operation Barbarossa, the Nazis take the room apart in about two hours, pack it into 27 crates within 36 hours, and move it by train to Königsberg Castle, where it is reassembled.

segments.title: Fate of the room: bombing and the Soviet advance
segments.summary: The RAF bombs Königsberg in July 1944. Alfred Rohde says the room was moved to safety and then returned after the raid. The Soviets take the city in April 1945, and in May the KGB finds the castle burned, with only fragments recovered.

segments.title: Theories about where the Amber Room went
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the official burned-in-castle account and competing theories: the Wilhelm Gustloff ship, the Jonas Valley tunnels, a Weimar train and bunkers, and the Vulpera mine. They also cover Rudy Voorst's sale of a fourth mosaic and George Stein's death.

segments.title: Modern replica in the Catherine Palace
segments.summary: In 1979 Soviet authorities commissioned a full-scale replica, which was opened to the public in 2003 after about 25 years of construction. The fourth mosaic, recovered through an illegal sale, is part of the replica. The replica is valued at about 500 million.

segments.title: Listener mail: toast water and toast sandwich
segments.summary: Listener Carl Rush from Victoria, Texas, writes about trying the toast sandwich and toast water from a previous episode with his son Henry. Carl's son spits out the toast water, but Carl likes it.
